title: SIREN: Software Identification and Recognition in HPC Systems
problem: HPC systems rely on monitoring and analytics for efficiency and security, but lack reliable software identification methods. Job/file names unreliable (user-provided). Application-specific insights hindered by inability to identify unknown software or recognize repeated executions across runs.
motivation: HPC workload diversity increasing; understanding applications critical for system optimization and security. Current identification methods (name-based) fail for arbitrary user naming. Need robust method preserving privacy while enabling workload analytics.
method: SIREN watches running programs and creates fingerprints of their code (called fuzzy hashes) that stay similar even when the program is updated or compiled differently. It collects basic information about each running process along with these fingerprints to recognize when the same program runs again, even if it looks different on the surface. The approach was tested on LUMI, a real supercomputer, with users able to opt in or out of sharing their data.
key_novelty: SIREN uses fuzzy hashing (fingerprints that stay similar across program versions) to identify running software at the process level in supercomputers, while letting users opt in to preserve privacy.
contributions: SIREN framework for process-level software identification
Fuzzy hashing approach for executable-based identification
Privacy-preserving analysis (fuzzy hash doesn't expose code)
Deployment and evaluation on LUMI supercomputer
Insights into software usage patterns and repeated execution recognition

metrics.focus: Identification accuracy, recognition of repeated executions, software diversity quantification

findings.ability: Provide insights into software usage patterns
findings.recognition: Identify repeated executions of known applications
findings.similarity: Identify unknown applications via fuzzy-hash similarity

limitations: Abstract only - no accuracy metrics, no false positive/negative rates, limited architectural detail on LUMI deployment
primary_theme: Workload characterization and identification in HPC systems
